name: Lectin-free diet

lead: The lectin-free diet removes foods high in lectins, carbohydrate-binding plant proteins found in beans, grains, tomatoes, potatoes and similar foods. It was popularized by cardiologist Steven Gundry in his 2017 book The Plant Paradox.

Followers report weight loss and less bloating, which feed into a leaner physique and better-looking skin. Authors and followers attribute this to reduced inflammation; reviewers cited by Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe the scientific support as limited.

paras: Followers swap legumes, wheat, nightshades and some fruit for leafy greens, pasture-raised meat, fish and certain oils, and may use pressure cooking or peeling for foods they keep. Programs usually run as a long-term eating pattern; Gundry also sells supplements.

The pattern removes fiber-rich foods and can be restrictive. Health organizations such as Harvard's school of public health and Mayo Clinic, as summarized in Grokipedia, caution about nutritional gaps. Raw kidney beans are genuinely toxic, but ordinary cooking removes most lectins.

lead: The lectin-free diet is an eating plan that excludes or heavily limits foods rich in lectins, which are carbohydrate-binding proteins common in legumes, grains, nightshades and some squashes.[1][2] Followers adopt it for weight loss, reduced bloating and what they describe as lower inflammation, outcomes tied to a leaner physique and clearer-looking skin.

The modern version was popularized by Steven Gundry, a former cardiothoracic surgeon, in The Plant Paradox (2017). Earlier, naturopath Peter D'Adamo included lectin avoidance in Eat Right 4 Your Type (1996).[1][2] Singer Kelly Clarkson publicly credited a Plant Paradox-style diet with weight loss in 2018.[1]

Lectins serve as plant defense proteins, and the first, ricin, was isolated in 1888.[1] Lab and animal work shows some lectins resist digestion and can affect the gut of animals when fed raw or concentrated.[3] Nutrition experts say cooking, soaking or fermenting inactivates most lectins in everyday food.[1][2]
infobox: Leafy greens, pasture-raised meat, certain fats

paras: Typical lists of avoided foods include beans, lentils, wheat, rice, tomatoes, potatoes, eggplant, peppers and some seeds, while leafy greens, certain oils and pasture-raised animal products are emphasized.[1] Variants allow pressure-cooked legumes or peeled, deseeded nightshades.[1]

Research from the mid twentieth century showed raw soybeans and kidney beans harmed growth and gut tissue in rats.[1] D'Adamo linked lectins to blood type in 1996.[1] Gundry's Plant Paradox in 2017, later books, social media and a supplement line made the diet widely known, and mainstream outlets covered it as a fad diet in 2018 and 2019.[1]

Wikipedia's lectin article reports that raw kidney beans contain toxic phytohaemagglutinin, that boiling or soaking removes most lectins, and that long-term health effects in humans have limited evidence; it also describes Gundry's claims as pseudoscience in its own words, which Gundry's supporters dispute.[4] Grokipedia says Harvard and Mayo Clinic experts recommend balanced plant-inclusive patterns instead.[1]
An animal feeding study of a seed lectin in rats showed the lectin resisted gut proteolysis and affected metabolism and gut tissue.[3]
No studies found. Animal work on plant lectins exists, for instance a rat feeding study,[3] but no controlled human trial has tested a lectin-free diet for appearance outcomes.
